    AI Overview
    +5
    The 1988 Seoul Olympics,
    held from September 17 to October 2 in South Korea, marked a major Cold War-era, "East-meets-West" gathering with 159 nations and 8,391 athletes participating. Known for the official motto "Harmony and Progress," the Games featured the mascot Hodori, a friendly tiger, and saw superstars like Florence Griffith Joyner dominate. 
    Key Details of the 1988 Seoul Olympics: 
    • Participation: 159 nations were represented, making it the largest turnout in Olympic history at the time.
    • Key Moments & Scandals: Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson's disqualification after winning the 100m gold in a world-record time (tested positive for steroids) became a massive, lasting scandal, with the gold awarded to Carl Lewis
      .
    • Motto: "Harmony and Progress" (화합과 전진).
    • Mascot: Hodori, a tiger dressed in traditional Korean clothing.
    • Theme Song: "Hand in Hand" by Koreana.
    • Closing Ceremony: Held on October 2, 1988, the closing featured a spectacular show, including a traditional "Talchum" masked dance and performances with massive, colorful costumes.
    • Closing by: IOC president Juan Antonio Samaranch formally closed the Games.
    • Significance: It was the second Summer Games in Asia and a pivotal, peaceful, and widely viewed event, signaling the decline of the Cold War and the rise of South Korea's international profile. 
    The games were a massive success for South Korea, which saw the event as a way to boost its global image beyond the Korean War. Despite a boycott from North Korea, Cuba, Ethiopia, and Nicaragua, the 1988 Games saw 52 nations taking home medals.

    AI Overview
    A total of 159 nations participated in the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul, South Korea. These Games, held from September 17 to October 2, 1988, were significant as the first major boycott-free Olympics in twelve years, featuring roughly 8,391 to 8,453 athletes. 
    Key Facts about 1988 Seoul Olympic Participation:
    • Participating Nations: 159. 
    • Athletes: ~8,391 athletes (6,197 men, 2,194 women). 
    • Boycotts: North Korea, Cuba, Ethiopia, and Nicaragua boycotted the Games. 
    • Significance: It was the largest Olympic Games in history at that time, with the USSR, USA, and both East and West Germany competing. 
    Note: Some sources may slightly differ on athlete numbers, but 159 is the widely cited number of participating nations..

      Closing Ceremony. What was the closing ceremony like for the Seoul Olympics?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      The 1988 Seoul Olympics closing ceremony was a vibrant celebration of Korean culture and a relieved, joyous farewell, featuring traditional dances like the Cymbal, Fan, and Lantern Dances. It featured massive, colorful choreography with up to 750 dancers on the stadium floor. Athletes celebrated informally, waving to crowds and dancing together, marking a successful, peaceful end to the Games. 
      Key highlights of the ceremony included:
      • Cultural Pageantry:
        The ceremony showcased Korean tradition with colorful performances, including lanterns and traditional ribbon-twirling dances. 
      • Informal Athlete Parade:
        Athletes entered the stadium together, often arm-in-arm and dancing, breaking from strict national lines to celebrate, with the South Korean delegation receiving the loudest cheers. 
      • Finality and Relief:
        Following a tense but successful competition, the atmosphere was one of celebration and relief, noted by organizers for its camaraderie. 
      • Official Handover:
        Seoul Mayor Kim Yong-rae handed the Olympic flag to IOC President Juan Antonio Samaranch, who passed it to Pasqual Maragall, the Mayor of Barcelona, host of the 1992 Summer Games. 
      • Formal Speeches:
        SLOOC President Park Seh-jik and IOC President Juan Antonio Samaranch delivered closing speeches, thanking the participants and organizers. 
      The ceremony concluded with the extinguishing of the Olympic flame, marking the end of the XXIV Olympiad.

        AI Overview
        The official motto of the 1988 Seoul Summer Olympics was "Harmony and Progress" (Korean: 화합과 전진). This motto was chosen to reflect the Olympic spirit of bringing together nations for peace and unity, while showcasing the development of mankind and the host country, South Korea. 
        Key details regarding the 1988 Seoul Olympics motto:
        • Significance:
          It aimed to promote harmony between different cultures and progress in the world, particularly after the boycotts of the previous three editions. 
        • Cultural Context:
          The motto reflected the Korean people's goal of fostering a peaceful, united world, often represented by the "Land of Morning Calm" imagery. 
        • Application:
          The theme was incorporated into the official posters, emblems, and the overall atmosphere of the Games, which saw high participation, including many countries from both sides of the Cold War.

          Mascot. What was the official mascot of the Seoul Olympics?
          About this result
          Feedback
          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          The official mascot of the 1988 Seoul Summer Olympic Games was Hodori, a stylized, friendly Amur tiger designed by Kim Hyun. Hodori, often depicted wearing the Olympic rings and a traditional sangmo hat, represented the hospitable traditions of the Korean people. A female version, Hosuni, was also introduced. 
          Key details about Hodori include:
          • Name Origin:
            "Ho" (호) comes from the Korean word for tiger (horangi), and "dori" (돌이) is a diminutive for boys. 
          • Selection:
            Chosen from thousands of suggestions in 1983, it was designed to be an amicable tiger rather than a scary one. 
          • Paralympics:
            The 1988 Summer Paralympics featured a different mascot called Gomdoori, a pair of Asian black bears.

            Medal Count. What was the medal count for the Seoul Olympics?
            About this result
            Feedback
            An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
            AI Overview
            At the 1988 Seoul Summer Olympics, the Soviet Union (USSR) led the overall medal count with 132 medals (55 gold), followed by East Germany with 102 medals (37 gold), and the United States with 94 medals (36 gold). Host nation South Korea finished fourth with 33 total medals. 
            Top Medal Standings (1988 Seoul Olympics):
            • Soviet Union (USSR): 55 Gold, 31 Silver, 46 Bronze = 132 Total 
            • East Germany (GDR): 37 Gold, 35 Silver, 30 Bronze = 102 Total 
            • United States (USA): 36 Gold, 31 Silver, 27 Bronze = 94 Total 
            • West Germany (FRG): 11 Gold, 14 Silver, 15 Bronze = 40 Total 
            • South Korea (KOR): 12 Gold, 10 Silver, 11 Bronze = 33 Total 
            A total of 525 gold, 515 silver, and 550 bronze medals were awarded across 237 events.
